title: I am, you are: the verb be
objective: Say who you are, where you're from and how you feel.

sections.heading: Forms of be
sections.en: I am · you are · he/she/it is · we/they are. Short forms: I'm, you're, he's.
sections.fr: Le verbe être. En anglais on dit « I am 20 » pour l'âge.

sections.heading: Questions
sections.en: Put be before the subject.
examples: Are you from Togo? — Yes, I am.
Is she a teacher? — No, she isn't.
Where are you from?

vocab.definition: shows where someone was born or lives
needing rest or sleep
feeling good
having a husband or wife

quiz.explanation: Short answers use the full form: Yes, I am.

title: Hello! Greetings and numbers
objective: Greet people, spell your name and use numbers 1–100.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.en: Hello / Hi · Good morning / afternoon / evening · Goodbye / Bye · Nice to meet you.
sections.fr: « Good night » sert seulement pour dire au revoir le soir ou avant de dormir.
examples: Hi, I'm Ama. Nice to meet you.
How are you? — I'm fine, thanks. And you?

sections.heading: Numbers
sections.en: 1–12: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve. Then thirteen… nineteen, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred.
sections.fr: Attention : thirteen (13) / thirty (30). L'accent est à la fin pour 13, au début pour 30.
examples: My number is 90 45 12 78.
She is thirteen. Her mother is thirty.

vocab.definition: polite words when you meet someone for the first time
vocab.example: Hi, Sam. Nice to meet you.

vocab.definition: well, OK
to say the letters of a word in order
vocab.example: How do you spell your name?

vocab.definition: the numbers you call to reach a phone

quiz.prompt: You say "Good night" when you arrive in the evening.
quiz.explanation: Arriving → Good evening. Good night = goodbye at night.
First meeting → Nice to meet you.

rememberErrors.why: Good night is only for leaving.

title: have got, my, your
objective: Talk about family and things you have with have got and possessive words.

sections.heading: have got
sections.en: I/you/we/they have got (I've got) · he/she has got (he's got). Negative: haven't got / hasn't got. Question: Have you got…?
sections.fr: « Have you got a car? » = As-tu une voiture ? On peut aussi dire « Do you have a car? ».
examples: I've got two brothers.
She hasn't got a car.
Have you got a pen?

sections.heading: Possessive words
sections.en: my · your · his · her · its · our · their. Name + 's = belongs to.
examples: This is my sister.
Ama's bag is red.

vocab.definition: a boy or man with the same parents as you
a girl or woman with the same parents as you
a thing you use to carry objects
a small metal object that opens a door

practice.prompt: This is Kofi. ___ car is blue.

quiz.prompt: He ___ got a bike. (negative, short form)
"the car of my father" is the natural way to say « la voiture de mon père ».

title: Family and jobs
objective: Name family members and say what people do.

sections.heading: Family
sections.en: mother · father · parents · son · daughter · brother · sister · husband · wife · grandmother · grandfather · uncle · aunt · cousin.
examples: My parents live in Kpalimé.
I've got two cousins in Accra.

sections.heading: Jobs
sections.en: Use a / an with jobs: I'm a teacher. She's an engineer. Ask: What do you do?
sections.fr: En anglais, l'article est obligatoire : « I am a nurse », pas « I am nurse ».
examples: What do you do? — I'm a student.
My father is a farmer.

vocab.definition: your mother and father
your female child
a person who grows food or keeps animals
a person who looks after sick people
vocab.example: She is a nurse in a hospital.

vocab.definition: a person who designs machines, roads or systems

quiz.explanation: What do you do? = What's your job?
Jobs need a/an: I am a teacher.

quiz.prompt: A person who grows food is a ___.

title: Present simple: my day
objective: Talk about your routine with the present simple.

sections.heading: Positive
sections.en: I/you/we/they work · he/she/it works. Add -es after -ch, -sh, -s, -o: watches, goes.
sections.fr: Le -s de la 3e personne est l'erreur n°1 des francophones.
examples: I get up at six.
She goes to work by bus.
He watches the news every evening.

sections.heading: Negative and questions
sections.en: don't / doesn't + verb. Do / Does + subject + verb?
examples: I don't drink coffee.
Does he work on Saturday? — Yes, he does.
What time do you start?

vocab.definition: to leave your bed in the morning
to eat the first meal of the day
to lie down to sleep
vocab.example: She goes to bed at ten.

vocab.definition: most of the time

quiz.prompt: We ___ (not / watch) TV in the morning.

quiz.explanation: After doesn't, no -s: She doesn't work.

quiz.answer: What time do you get up

title: Days, months and the time
objective: Say the time, the days of the week and dates.

sections.heading: The time
sections.en: It's seven o'clock · half past seven (7:30) · quarter past seven (7:15) · quarter to eight (7:45). Ask: What time is it?
sections.fr: « Half past seven » = 7 h 30 : on compte à partir de l'heure passée.
examples: What time is it? — It's half past three.
The bank opens at nine o'clock.

sections.heading: Days and months
sections.en: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. January… December. Always a capital letter. on + day, in + month.
examples: See you on Friday.
My birthday is in August.

vocab.definition: used for exact hours
thirty minutes after the hour
Saturday and Sunday
vocab.example: What do you do at the weekend?

vocab.definition: the day you were born, every year

quiz.prompt: In English, days and months start with a capital letter.

quiz.explanation: 15 minutes before ten → quarter to ten.

title: There is, there are: my town
objective: Describe a place with there is / there are and prepositions of place.

sections.heading: there is / there are
sections.en: There is (there's) + one thing. There are + many things. Questions: Is there…? Are there…? Use any in questions and negatives.
sections.fr: « Il y a » = there is / there are. Ne dites pas « it has ».
examples: There's a market near my house.
There are three hotels in the town.
Is there a bank here? — No, there isn't.
There aren't any taxis.

sections.heading: Where is it?
sections.en: in · on · under · next to · between · opposite · near.
examples: The pharmacy is next to the bank.
The keys are on the table.
The school is opposite the church.

vocab.definition: a place where people buy and sell food and goods
vocab.example: There's a big market in the centre.

vocab.definition: a shop that sells medicine
vocab.example: Is there a pharmacy near here?

vocab.definition: very close, at the side of
vocab.example: The bank is next to the hotel.

vocab.definition: on the other side, facing
vocab.example: The school is opposite the church.

quiz.prompt: There ___ a supermarket near the station.
"It has a pharmacy in my street" is natural English.
quiz.explanation: Use There is a pharmacy in my street.

quiz.prompt: The bank is ___ the pharmacy and the hotel.
quiz.explanation: In the middle of two places → between.

rememberErrors.why: « Il y a » = there is / there are.

title: Shopping and prices
objective: Ask for things, ask the price and pay in a shop.

sections.heading: In a shop
sections.en: Can I have…, please? · How much is it / are they? · That's 500 francs. · Here you are. · Thank you.
sections.fr: « How much » pour le prix. « Can I have » est poli et très courant.
examples: Can I have two bottles of water, please?
How much are these shoes? — They're 15,000 francs.
Here you are. — Thank you!

sections.heading: this, that, these, those
sections.en: this / these = near you; that / those = far from you. Singular: this, that. Plural: these, those.
examples: How much is this shirt?
I like those bags.

vocab.definition: used to ask a price
not expensive
vocab.example: Fruit is cheap at the market.

vocab.definition: costing a lot of money
money you get back when you pay too much

quiz.prompt: Polite way to ask for water:
options: Can I have some water, please?

quiz.prompt: "Here you are" is what you say when you give something to someone.
Money you get back is the…

rememberErrors.right: How much does it cost? / How much is it?
Can I have some bread, please?

title: some, any, how much, how many

sections.heading: Countable or not?
sections.en: Countable: one apple, two apples. Uncountable: water, rice, bread, money — no plural, no a/an.
sections.fr: « Du riz » = some rice. On ne dit jamais « a rice » ni « rices ».
examples: I've got some bananas.
There's some rice in the pot.

sections.heading: some / any · much / many
sections.en: some in positive sentences; any in questions and negatives. How many + plural; How much + uncountable.
examples: Is there any milk?
We haven't got any eggs.
How many eggs? How much sugar?

vocab.definition: small white or brown grains you cook and eat
a glass or plastic container for liquids
food made from flour and baked

practice.prompt: There is ___ water in the fridge.

rememberErrors.right: some bread / a piece of bread

title: Food and meals
objective: Name food and drinks and order a meal.

sections.heading: Meals
sections.en: breakfast (morning) · lunch (midday) · dinner (evening). I'd like… is polite for ordering.
examples: For breakfast I have tea and bread.
I'd like chicken and rice, please.

sections.heading: Food words
sections.en: fish · chicken · meat · vegetables · fruit · beans · soup · juice · water · tea · coffee.
sections.fr: « I'd like » = je voudrais. Plus poli que « I want ».

vocab.definition: the meal in the middle of the day
plants you eat, like tomatoes or carrots
a drink made from fruit
wanting to eat

quiz.prompt: Juice is a drink made from fruit.

rememberErrors.wrong: I want a coffee. (to a waiter)

title: can, like and love + -ing
objective: Say what you can do and what you like doing.

sections.heading: can / can't
sections.en: can + verb for ability, the same for all persons. Can you…? — Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
examples: I can swim, but I can't dance.
Can you play the guitar?

sections.heading: like / love / hate + -ing
sections.en: After like, love, hate and enjoy, use the -ing form.
examples: She loves cooking.
I don't like getting up early.
Do you enjoy reading?

vocab.definition: to like doing something
to really not like
to move through water

title: Free time and weather
objective: Talk about hobbies and the weather.

sections.heading: Hobbies
sections.en: play football / cards · go swimming / shopping · watch films · listen to music · read books.
examples: At the weekend I play football.
We go shopping on Saturday.

sections.heading: Weather
sections.en: It's sunny · hot · cold · windy · raining · cloudy. Ask: What's the weather like?
examples: What's the weather like today? — It's hot and sunny.
It's raining. Take an umbrella!

vocab.definition: Saturday and Sunday
vocab.example: What do you do at the weekend?

vocab.definition: with a lot of sun
a thing that protects you from rain
something you like doing in your free time

practice.prompt: Lots of water from the sky:

quiz.prompt: "It's windy" means there is a lot of wind.
Something you like doing in your free time is a…

rememberErrors.right: I do sport. / I play football.
